trips.description:
At midnight you leave Barafu Camp at 15,331 ft (4,673 m). About eight hours later you watch the sun rise from Uhuru Peak, 19,341 ft (5,895 m), the highest point in Africa and one of the Seven Summits.

No technical climbing, no ropes, no crampons. If you can hike six to eight hours a day and train for about three months, you can do this. 94% of HighAir climbers reach the summit.

We climb the Machame Route over seven days, with a built-in acclimatization day so your body adjusts before summit night. Experienced local guides check every climber's health each morning, the group carries emergency oxygen and satellite communication, and a crew of cooks and porters handles everything except the walking.

Small groups of up to 15 climbers from around the world, guided in English. Part of the proceeds from every expedition supports cancer patients, because for us, the mountains are also a way to give back.

faq.q: How hard is it to climb Kilimanjaro?
faq.a: Kilimanjaro (5,895 m) is the most accessible high mountain in the world - no technical climbing experience, ropes or crampons needed. Anyone in reasonable shape who can walk about eight hours a day can reach the summit. The real challenge is the altitude and the cold on summit night, which is exactly why our itinerary is built around proper acclimatization.

faq.q: What is your Kilimanjaro success rate?
faq.a: Our summit success rate is 94%, one of the highest in the industry. It comes from choosing the scenic Machame Route over 7 days, which gives the body time to acclimatize gradually, and from experienced local guides who know every stretch of the mountain and when to push and when to rest.

faq.q: How do I prepare for climbing Kilimanjaro?
faq.a: The most important preparation is aerobic: long hikes, light running or cycling over about three months before departure. Before departure the group also meets online for a gear briefing and a preparation call, so you reach the mountain ready and already knowing each other.

faq.q: What is the minimum age for Kilimanjaro?
faq.a: The minimum age is 10. There is no maximum - climbers in their 60s and beyond have summited with us. What matters is fitness and health, not the number on your ID.

faq.q: Is it worth adding a safari to a Kilimanjaro climb?
faq.a: Absolutely. Three safari days in Tarangire and the Ngorongoro Crater, two of Africa's most spectacular reserves, can be added for a reasonable extra cost. After a hard week on the mountain, the safari is the perfect reward.

faq.q: When is the best season to climb Kilimanjaro?
faq.a: Two preferred seasons: January-February and June-October. In these months rain is light and the weather more stable. It is best to avoid November and April, the heavy rain months - and we run our groups precisely in the good windows.

trips.description:
The Everest Base Camp trek is one of the most iconic and exhilarating routes in the Himalayas. The journey begins in Lukla and winds through breathtaking scenery of rivers, forests and wildlife, passing authentic Sherpa villages and rich Buddhist culture.

Base Camp itself sits at 5364m above sea level — the very starting point for climbers attempting the summit of Everest. The trek also includes the dramatic Cho La Pass crossing, the unique village of Gokyo and its stunning glacial lakes, offering views found nowhere else on earth.

Along the way you'll be surrounded by the great Himalayan peaks: Everest, Lhotse, Nuptse and many more. The route culminates at Kala Patthar (5545m) — one of the world's most spectacular viewpoints for a sunrise over Everest. An unforgettable experience of power and altitude.

Join us for a once-in-a-lifetime adventure in the Himalayas and take part in the fight against cancer!

faq.q: How high do you go on the Everest Base Camp trek?
faq.a: The highest point on the trek is Kala Patthar (5,545 m), which offers a stunning panorama of Everest; Base Camp itself sits at 5,364 m. These are the heights that challenge the body's acclimatization, which is why our itinerary is built carefully with rest days.

faq.q: Is altitude sickness a real risk on the trek?
faq.a: Altitude sickness is the main challenge on the Everest Base Camp trek - about a third of trekkers feel mild symptoms such as headache and fatigue. That is why we dedicate 19 days to the journey, with acclimatization days in Namche Bazaar and Dingboche. Drinking plenty, ascending gradually and watching for symptoms are the keys.

faq.q: What fitness level does the EBC trek require?
faq.a: You need good fitness, but not that of a professional athlete. The key is being able to walk 5-7 hours a day with a daypack, day after day, over two weeks. The best preparation is long hikes with a pack in the months before - the difficulty is cumulative, not technical.

faq.q: Can you see the summit of Everest from Base Camp?
faq.a: Actually no - from Base Camp itself the glacier blocks the view of the summit. The best place to see Everest is Kala Patthar (5,545 m), from where the view of Everest, Lhotse and Nuptse is among the most spectacular in the world.

faq.q: When is the best season to trek in Nepal?
faq.a: Two excellent seasons: April-May before the monsoon, and October-November after it. In both the skies are clear, the scenery breathtaking and the weather relatively comfortable - and we aim for exactly those. It is best to avoid the monsoon months (June-September).

faq.q: Is the Everest Base Camp trek suitable for beginners?
faq.a: Yes, if you come prepared. It is a trek, not a technical climb: no ropes or ice axe, and crampons are needed only when there is snow on the trail. What it takes is cardiovascular endurance, mental readiness for altitude and the right gear. Many trekkers with no prior experience have completed it successfully with us.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Annapurna Circuit and the Everest Base Camp trek?
faq.a: The Annapurna Circuit is more varied in scenery and culture - it crosses villages of different styles, forests and passes, while Everest Base Camp is more focused on the altitude challenge and the "heart of the Himalayas" feeling. Annapurna is perfect for the full Nepal experience; EBC for when altitude is the goal.

faq.q: What is the highest point on the Annapurna Circuit?
faq.a: The highest point is the Thorong La Pass (5,416 m), one of the highest mountain passes in the world crossed on foot. The pre-dawn ascent to it, into a sunrise view above the clouds of Nepal, is the highlight of the trek and an experience that stays with you.

faq.q: Is the trek clockwise or counter-clockwise?
faq.a: We walk the circuit anticlockwise, up the Marsyangdi valley and through Manang to the Thorong La Pass, then down to Muktinath. This makes the ascent to the pass gradual and allows better acclimatization, and from Muktinath we drive by jeep to Pokhara.

faq.q: Do I need experience for the Annapurna Circuit?
faq.a: No climbing experience is needed. Anyone who can walk 6-8 hours a day and arrives in reasonable shape can complete the trek. The main challenge is the Thorong La Pass, which requires a start in the dark and a long ascent - and our guides prepare you for it along the way.

faq.q: What is included in the Annapurna Circuit and what is not?
faq.a: Included: transfers, lodge accommodation, three meals a day, a guide and the area entry permits. Not included: international flights, travel insurance, the Nepal visa ($50) and personal gear. A detailed gear list is sent after registration.

This extraordinary journey through Ethiopia runs from the spectacular Simien Mountains trek, through the prehistoric Danakil Desert and the colorful Dallol Depression, all the way to the ancient rock-hewn churches of Tigray.

Our adventure begins in the Simien Mountains National Park, home to some of Africa's most dramatic landscapes. We trek between breathtaking cliffs, summit peaks over 4000m, and encounter Gelada baboons, the endemic Walia ibex and the rare Ethiopian wolf in their natural habitat.

We close the journey in Tigray, climbing up to the rock-hewn churches - one of Ethiopia's best-kept secrets, carved directly into towering cliff faces over a thousand years ago.

Join us on this incredible Ethiopian adventure and make a meaningful contribution to the fight against cancer!

faq.q: What should I check before travelling to Ethiopia?
faq.a: As before any trip abroad, check the current travel recommendations for Israelis before registering and again before departure, and make sure your travel insurance covers every area on the route. Our local team knows the country deeply and accompanies the group throughout the journey.

faq.q: How dangerous is it to approach the Erta Ale lava lake?
faq.a: Access to the Erta Ale lava lake is done with experienced local guides and a security escort, and you stand at the crater rim from a safe distance. It is one of the rarest experiences on earth - watching boiling lava at night - and the high level of safety is what makes it accessible.

faq.q: What is the maximum altitude on the Ethiopia trip?
faq.a: The maximum altitude is the summit of Ras Bwahit in the Simien Mountains (4,430 m). By contrast, the Erta Ale volcano rises only 613 m, in the heart of the Danakil Depression, parts of which lie below sea level. The high section in the Simiens can cause mild altitude symptoms, so we built the itinerary with gradual acclimatization.

faq.q: What vaccinations are required for Ethiopia?
faq.a: Vaccinations are required. Mandatory: yellow fever (checked on entry) and typhoid; several others are recommended and detailed in the medical document sent after registration. It is worth visiting a travel clinic at least six weeks before the flight.

faq.q: What is the recommended season for Ethiopia?
faq.a: The best season is November to February, the dry winter. The Simien Mountains are green and beautiful, and the weather in Danakil is relatively bearable (35-40°C instead of 50 in summer) - and we run our journeys precisely in this window.

faq.q: How is the Ethiopia trip different from your other treks?

faq.q: How hard is Aconcagua compared to Kilimanjaro?
faq.a: Aconcagua is significantly harder. It is the highest peak outside Asia (6,962 m) and the expedition runs 20 days - the altitude is higher, the cold sharper, and you carry heavy gear up to Camp 2. Prior experience at an altitude of at least 5,000 m, such as Kilimanjaro or the Everest Base Camp trek, is required.

faq.q: How much is the Aconcagua permit?
faq.a: The Aconcagua Provincial Park permit costs about $1,000 to $1,300 per person, depending on the season and route. It is not included in the price and is paid directly to the park authority; we guide you through the purchase and all the required paperwork.

faq.q: Do I need technical climbing experience for Aconcagua?
faq.a: No. The Normal Route, which we climb, is a walking route rather than a technical climb - no ropes and no crampons (unless it snows). That said, the high altitude and extreme cold demand prior altitude experience and quality warm gear.

faq.q: When is the Aconcagua climbing season?
faq.a: The season is December to February, the southern-hemisphere summer, when the peak can be climbed in the safest conditions. Outside that window the mountain is officially closed. We run one expedition a year, in January, at the heart of the season.

faq.q: What is the success rate on Aconcagua?
faq.a: The overall success rate on Aconcagua is only about 40%; ours is 75%, well above average. The secret is a carefully paced acclimatization schedule, a guide who knows the mountain intimately, and choosing the right climbers for summit day.

faq.q: Is Elbrus harder than Kilimanjaro?
faq.a: Elbrus is more technical. At a similar height (5,642 m) it requires walking on crampons with an ice axe, the cold is harsher, and sudden storms are a risk. Our summit success rate is 85%, versus 94% on Kilimanjaro. Our recommendation: if this is your first high peak, start with Kilimanjaro.

faq.q: Do I need experience to climb Elbrus?
faq.a: You need basic experience walking on snow and in crampons, but not technical climbing. On the first day at base camp we run crampon practice and training on the snow slopes, and anyone who has already been to altitude - Kilimanjaro, for example - arrives with a physical and mental advantage.

faq.q: How cold is the Elbrus summit?
faq.a: On summit night the temperature usually drops to between -15° and -25°C, and with wind chill it can feel like -35°C. That makes warm gloves, thermal layers, a face mask (balaclava) and good ski goggles essential. A full gear list is sent to every registrant.

faq.q: What is the entry situation to Russia for Israelis?
faq.a: Israelis enter Russia without a visa, with a valid passport, for stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Entry rules can change, so check them before booking and again before your flight.

faq.q: What technical gear do you provide?
faq.a: We provide every participant with crampons, an ice axe and a harness on loan, at no extra cost - there is no need to buy expensive climbing gear. All you need to bring is basic warm clothing, mountain boots with a stiff sole, and a sleeping setup suited to altitude.

trips.description:
Manaslu, the "Mountain of the Spirit," rises to 8163 meters in the heart of the Himalayas in Nepal, the eighth-highest mountain on earth and one of the 14 highest peaks in the world above 8000 meters. For experienced climbers, Manaslu is the gateway to the world of the 8000ers: a serious high-altitude expedition, one that welcomes those who have already stood on 6000 and 7000 meter peaks.

The way to base camp winds through remote villages and deep valleys at the foot of the range, far from the crowded trekking trails. From there the climb itself begins: acclimatization and rotations between the high camps, glacier travel past crevasses, and fixed-rope climbing toward the summit. The moment you ascend above eight thousand meters, an endless horizon of Himalayan peaks opens before you. It is a place only a few in the world ever reach!

trips.description:
Ama Dablam is one of the most beautiful and recognizable peaks in the Himalayas, rising to 6812 meters above sea level. It sits in the Khumbu region of Nepal, close to Everest, and is considered one of the most sought-after technical climbing peaks in the world.

Its sharp, elegant shape earned it the nickname "the Matterhorn of the Himalayas," and its name, "Mother's Necklace," comes from the hanging glacier on its flanks that looks like a pendant on the mother's neck.

The route to the summit climbs the south-west ridge and combines rock, ice and mixed climbing, with exposed sections and fixed ropes along the way. The trek to base camp passes through the Khumbu valley, past Sherpa villages and monasteries, with views of Everest and Lhotse.

The climb requires good fitness, previous technical climbing experience and acclimatization to altitude, and it suits experienced climbers looking for a genuine technical challenge in the Himalayas.

Join us on a journey to one of the most beautiful peaks in the world and take a meaningful part in the fight against cancer!

trips.description:
Himlung Himal is an impressive climbing peak in the Himalayas, rising to 7126 meters above sea level. It sits in the remote Nar-Phu valley in northern Nepal, near the Tibetan border, in the region between Manaslu and Annapurna.

Himlung is considered one of the best peaks in the world for a first climb at 7000 meters, and it serves as excellent preparation for expeditions to the eight-thousanders.

The trek to base camp passes through remote valleys and Tibetan-style villages, far from the tourist trails. The climb itself involves acclimatization rotations between the high camps, crossing snow slopes and glaciers, and using fixed ropes on the way to the summit.

The climb requires good fitness, previous mountaineering experience and acclimatization to altitude, but it is considered relatively accessible and suits climbers looking for a first taste of climbing at 7000 meters.

Join us on a journey to your first 7000m peak and take a meaningful part in the fight against cancer!
